c.tagline: A UNESCO-listed Saharan oasis of five fortified ochre-and-white M'Zab valley towns
langs: French (widely used in business and signage)

card: Rarely accepted outside major hotels; cash is essential throughout the M'Zab valley

taxi.fare: Negotiated flat rate, as meters are uncommon
taxi.fareNote: Agree the fare before departure; hiring a taxi with a local guide for the day is common for touring the five ksour

emergency.note: Dial 17 for police and 14 for medical/fire emergencies; English is rarely spoken by dispatchers, French is more useful

religion: Islam (Sunni majority, with a significant Ibadi Muslim community distinctive to the M'Zab valley)
walk: Each of the five ksour (walled towns) is walkable on its own steep, maze-like streets, but distances between them require a taxi or car

safety.safety: Generally safe for visitors traveling with a local guide, though Algeria's south requires more planning than typical tourist destinations
safety.crime: Violent crime against tourists is rare; the bigger practical challenges are limited English, cash-only transactions, and conservative local customs to respect (modest dress, guide requirements in Beni Isguen)

hood_landmark.Ghardaïa Medina: The 10th-century Ghardaïa Mosque and its pyramidal minaret
hood_landmark.Beni Isguen: Beni Isguen's strictly preserved walled old town
hood_landmark.Melika: Melika's hilltop cemetery overlooking the valley
hood_landmark.El Atteuf: El Atteuf's ancient mosque, an architectural precursor to modernist design

avoid.reason: There are no true no-go zones, but the holy walled town of Beni Isguen is entry-restricted — non-residents must enter with a local guide, photography of people is forbidden, and it closes to outsiders at prayer times.

Be discreet with cameras (locals, especially Mozabite women, must not be photographed) and keep valuables secure in the souk; check current conditions given past communal tensions in the M'zab valley.

hood_desc: The largest and richest of the five M'Zab towns, with the main market, mosque, and most hotels; the practical base for exploring the valley.
The most conservative and best-preserved of the five ksour, still closing its gates to non-residents at night; visits require a local guide.
A smaller hilltop town known for its panoramic cemetery and sweeping views over the whole M'Zab valley.
One of the smaller, quieter ksour with a compact fortified core, less visited than Ghardaïa or Beni Isguen.
The oldest of the five towns, its 11th-century mosque cited as an influence on modernist architect Le Corbusier.

water.note: Drink bottled water; tap water in the Saharan south is not reliable for visitors.

transit.sys: Local shared taxis and minibuses connecting the five ksour towns
transit.hours: Roughly daylight hours; travel after dark is uncommon
transit.map: Not centrally published; hotels and guides arrange transport between towns
transit.note: Alcohol is not sold locally (Beni Isguen and much of the valley is dry); a licensed local guide is required to enter Beni Isguen's old town

transport.air: Noumérat - Moufdi Zakaria Airport (GHA), serving Ghardaïa with domestic flights from Algiers
transport.train: No passenger rail service to Ghardaïa
transport.bus: Long-distance buses connect Ghardaïa to Algiers (roughly 6-7 hr) and other southern Algerian towns
transport.car: The N1 highway connects Ghardaïa to Algiers; a guide or organized tour is recommended for independent travelers

net.m: Moderate 3G/4G coverage in town, weaker in the surrounding desert
net.w: Wifi available in hotels but often slow
net.gb: ~$5-10 for a prepaid tourist SIM (foreign registration can require passport and patience)
net.fwn: Wifi available in most hotels, though connection quality varies
net.ap: A Mobilis or Djezzy prepaid SIM, registered with your passport

tip.s: 10% is appreciated for local guides, required for entry to Beni Isguen
tip.r: Rounding up or 5-10% is appreciated, not obligatory
